native_result.query: How is the advantage in BA degree completion rates for Black students related to Socioeconomic status levels?
native_result.HypoA: The advantage in BA degree completion rates for Black students is more pronounced at lower SES levels with the interaction term for Socioeconomic status and being black having a coefficient of 0.7606
native_result.HypoB: In this NLSY79 extract, Black students do NOT show an advantage in BA (or proxy) completion relative to non-Black, non-Hispanic students. The only attainment variable is baseline 1979 highest grade; using grade>=16 as a BA proxy (n=37 overall), Black completion is at or below the reference group in every 1979-income tercile. At more common thresholds (high-school >=12, some-college >=13), Black students show a consistent attainment DISADVANTAGE that is largest at low SES and monotonically narrows as family income rises (HS gap: -30pp lowest tercile -> -6pp highest; some-college: -10.4pp -> -2.5pp). The question's premise of a Black advantage does not hold in this dataset; the real relationship is a SES-moderated racial gap that attenuates with SES.
native_result.WorkflowB: Loaded nls_raw.csv (N=12686); confirmed no degree/BA indicator, only baseline 1979 highest grade (95 treated as missing). Defined BA proxy grade>=16 (declared as baseline, not later degree outcome) plus robust thresholds >=12/>=13. SES primary window = 1979 family income terciles (cutpoints 7000/17000); reference group = non-Black non-Hispanic. Complete-case analysis with before/after sample-size reporting. Primary inference = descriptive Black-vs-reference rate differences and ratios with Wilson 95% CIs within each SES stratum; logistic Black*income interaction (HS>=12) as secondary reference; wealth windows and parent-education as SES sensitivity. Concluded: no advantage; a SES-moderated gap that narrows with SES.
